name: Ascorbic acid
text:
Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. It occurs naturally in fruit and vegetables; the food additive is produced industrially, mostly from glucose by fermentation and chemical steps.

It is used as an antioxidant to slow oxidation and browning and to prevent discolouration during storage, for example in canned fruit. It is also used as a flour treatment agent in breadmaking and is added to cured meat, where it reduces the formation of nitrosamines.

In its 2015 re-evaluation EFSA found no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels.

name: Sodium ascorbate
text:
Sodium ascorbate is the sodium salt of ascorbic acid (vitamin C). It is made by neutralising ascorbic acid with sodium hydroxide or sodium bicarbonate, and is less acidic than ascorbic acid itself.

It is used as an antioxidant and acidity regulator, mainly to prevent oxidation and discolouration during storage; ascorbate is also added to cured meats. It is one of the common forms of vitamin C in supplements.

In its 2015 re-evaluation EFSA found no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels.

name: Calcium ascorbate
text:
Calcium ascorbate is the calcium salt of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and is about 10% calcium by mass.

It is used as an antioxidant food additive, mainly to prevent oxidation and discolouration of products during storage. It is also one of the common forms of vitamin C in supplements.

In its 2015 re-evaluation EFSA found no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels.

name: Potassium ascorbate
text: Potassium ascorbate is the potassium salt of ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Like ascorbic acid and its sodium and calcium salts, it acts as a water-soluble antioxidant.

name: Fatty acid esters of ascorbic acid
text:
These are esters of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) with fatty acids: ascorbyl palmitate and ascorbyl stearate. They are made synthetically by acylating ascorbic acid. Unlike ascorbic acid and its salts, they dissolve in fats.

They are used as antioxidants to protect fats and oils, and foods containing them, from oxidation.

In its 2015 re-evaluation EFSA found no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels, assuming the esters are fully broken down in the gut to ascorbic acid and fatty acids.

name: Ascorbyl stearate
text:
Ascorbyl stearate is an ester of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and stearic acid. Unlike ascorbic acid, it dissolves in fats.

It is used as an antioxidant food additive, for example in margarine. In the EU it is covered by E304(ii) as one of the fatty acid esters of ascorbic acid, and the code E305 is not used there.

In the US, USDA rules limit its use in margarine to 0.02%, alone or together with other antioxidants.

name: Tocopherol-rich extract
text:
Tocopherol-rich extract is a mixture of tocopherols (forms of vitamin E) of natural origin, extracted from vegetable oils.

Tocopherols are fat-soluble antioxidants: they neutralise free radicals and so protect fats and oils, and foods containing them, from oxidation.

In its 2015 re-evaluation of E306 to E309, EFSA concluded that tocopherols are not of safety concern at the levels used in food.

name: Alpha-tocopherol
text:
Alpha-tocopherol is the most biologically active form of vitamin E. The food additive is synthetic alpha-tocopherol, a mixture of stereoisomers that is less active as a vitamin than the natural form.

It is used as a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects fats and oils from oxidation.

In its 2015 re-evaluation EFSA concluded that alpha-tocopherol is not of safety concern at the reported uses and use levels as a food additive.

name: Gamma-tocopherol
text:
Gamma-tocopherol is one of the tocopherols, the compounds that make up vitamin E. It is the main form of vitamin E in the American diet, coming largely from soybean and corn oil. The food additive is the synthetic form.

It is used as a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects fats and oils from oxidation. It is used at much lower levels and in fewer foods than alpha-tocopherol.

EFSA concluded in 2015 that tocopherols (E306 to E309) are not of safety concern at the levels used in food.

name: Delta-tocopherol
text:
Delta-tocopherol is one of the tocopherols, the compounds that make up vitamin E. The food additive is the synthetic form.

It is used as a fat-soluble antioxidant that slows the oxidation of fats and oils. It is used at much lower levels and in fewer foods than alpha-tocopherol.

EFSA concluded in 2015 that tocopherols (E306 to E309) are not of safety concern at the levels used in food.

name: Propyl gallate
text:
Propyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid and propanol. It does not occur naturally and is made synthetically.

It has been added to foods containing oils and fats since 1948 to protect them from oxidation. It is also used in cosmetics and other products for the same purpose.

In its 2014 re-evaluation EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 0.5 mg per kg of body weight and concluded that its use at current levels is not of safety concern.

name: Octyl gallate
text:
Octyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid and octanol. It is used as an antioxidant in foods such as margarine and peanut butter, and in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals; it works synergistically with BHA and BHT.

The EU removed octyl gallate from its list of food additives in 2018: EFSA could not confirm its safety for lack of adequate toxicological data, and no business operator offered to supply them.

name: Dodecyl gallate
text:
Dodecyl gallate, also called lauryl gallate, is an ester of gallic acid and dodecanol (lauryl alcohol). It has been used as an antioxidant and preservative in foods.

The EU removed dodecyl gallate from its list of food additives in 2018: EFSA could not confirm its safety for lack of adequate toxicological data, and no business operator offered to supply them.

name: Ethyl gallate
text:
Ethyl gallate is the ethyl ester of gallic acid. It occurs naturally in some plants, such as walnuts, and in wine, but for use as a food additive it is made from gallic acid and ethanol.

It is added to food as an antioxidant.

name: Guaiac resin
text:
Guaiac resin (gum guaiacum) is a natural resin obtained from the tree Guaiacum officinale. It is a mixture made up mainly of guaiaconic acids, with guaiaretic acid and other compounds.

As a food additive it is classed as an antioxidant. It is also used in medicine in the stool guaiac test for hidden blood.

name: Erythorbic acid
text:
Erythorbic acid, also called isoascorbic acid, is a stereoisomer of ascorbic acid (vitamin C). It is produced industrially from glucose by microbial fermentation followed by a chemical step.

It is used as an antioxidant in processed foods, for example cured meats and frozen vegetables. In cured meat, like ascorbic acid, it helps form the typical pink colour and reduces the formation of nitrosamines.

In its 2016 re-evaluation EFSA kept the acceptable daily intake of 6 mg per kg of body weight and found no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Sodium erythorbate
text:
Sodium erythorbate is the sodium salt of erythorbic acid, a stereoisomer of ascorbic acid. It is made from sugars (from beet, cane or corn) that bacteria convert to an intermediate acid.

It is used mainly in meat and poultry products and in soft drinks. In cured meats such as hot dogs it speeds up curing, keeps the pink colour and prevents the formation of nitrosamines.

In its 2016 re-evaluation EFSA kept the acceptable daily intake of 6 mg per kg of body weight and found no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Potassium erythorbate
text: Potassium erythorbate, also called potassium isoascorbate, is the potassium salt of erythorbic acid, a stereoisomer of ascorbic acid (vitamin C). It is an antioxidant food additive. Erythorbates are used to improve flavour stability and to prevent the formation of nitrosamines.

name: Calcium erythorbate
text: Calcium erythorbate, also called calcium isoascorbate, is the calcium salt of erythorbic acid, a stereoisomer of ascorbic acid (vitamin C). It is an antioxidant food additive. Erythorbates are used to improve flavour stability and to prevent the formation of nitrosamines.

name: Tertiary-butylhydroquinone (TBHQ)
text:
Tertiary-butylhydroquinone (TBHQ) is a synthetic phenolic compound derived from hydroquinone.

It is used as an antioxidant for unsaturated vegetable oils and edible animal fats, to extend storage life. It does not discolour food even in the presence of iron and does not change flavour or odour, and it can be combined with BHA. In the EU and the US its level is limited to 0.02% of the fat or oil content.

Very high doses have caused harmful effects in laboratory animals; reviews found a wide margin between these doses and intake from food.

name: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA)
text:
Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) is a synthetic antioxidant, a mixture of two isomers made from 4-methoxyphenol and isobutylene.

Since about 1947 it has been added to fats and fat-containing foods to prevent rancidity, and it is also used in food packaging, animal feed and cosmetics. It is often combined with BHT.

High doses cause forestomach tumours in rats and hamsters. In its 2011 re-evaluation EFSA considered these effects possibly no longer relevant to humans, who have no forestomach, and set an acceptable daily intake of 1.0 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT)
text:
Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) is a fat-soluble antioxidant derived from phenol and made industrially from p-cresol and isobutylene. It acts much like a synthetic analogue of vitamin E, stopping the oxidation of fats by trapping free radicals.

It is used as a food preservative to slow changes in colour, flavour and texture, and also in cosmetics, medicines, fuels and plastics. It is sometimes used together with BHA.

Animal studies on cancer have given mixed results. In 2012 EFSA found no genotoxicity concern and set an acceptable daily intake of 0.25 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Lecithins
text:
Lecithins are natural mixtures of phospholipids. For food use they are obtained mainly from soybean oil, and also from sunflower, rapeseed and egg yolk.

They are emulsifiers that help oil and water mix. In chocolate and confectionery they control flow and sugar crystallisation; in margarine they stabilise the emulsion and reduce spattering during frying.

Soy lecithin usually contains too little soy protein to affect most people with soy allergy. EFSA concluded in 2017 that lecithins raise no safety concern at reported uses and need no numerical acceptable daily intake.

name: Oat lecithin
text:
Oat lecithin is a fraction of oat oil rich in polar lipids, obtained from oats by extraction with ethanol followed by fractionation. It acts as an emulsifier.

The EU added it to its list of food additives in 2022 for use in cocoa and chocolate products. There it lowers the viscosity of molten chocolate, making it easier to pump, and helps prevent fat bloom, a greyish haze on the surface, during storage.

In 2020 EFSA noted that it is broken down in the gut like other edible vegetable oils, saw no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and found no safety concern at the proposed use.

name: Anoxomer
text:
Anoxomer is a synthetic polymeric antioxidant that is not digested. It was designed to deliver established antioxidants in a form the body does not absorb, to avoid possible health risks from absorbing them.

It is made by polymerising divinylbenzene with antioxidant monomers such as tert-butylhydroquinone and tert-butylphenol.

name: Ethoxyquin
text:
Ethoxyquin is a synthetic quinoline-based antioxidant. It was first used to prevent scald on stored pears, and is used in some pet foods to slow rancidity, in some spices to stop colour loss, and in fish meal to prevent fires. In the US, its use as a food additive is limited to chili powder, paprika and ground chili.

In 2015 EFSA could not assess its safety for consumers as a feed additive: one metabolite may be genotoxic and an impurity, p-phenetidine, is a possible mutagen. The EU suspended it as a feed additive in 2017.

name: Sodium lactate
text:
Sodium lactate is the sodium salt of lactic acid and has a mildly salty taste. It is made by fermenting a sugar source such as maize or beet and neutralising the resulting lactic acid.

As a food additive it acts as a preservative, acidity regulator and bulking agent.

Despite its name it is not related to lactose (milk sugar) and contains no milk protein, so it need not be avoided by people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

name: Potassium lactate
text:
Potassium lactate is the potassium salt of lactic acid. It is made by neutralising lactic acid fermented from a sugar source, and is usually supplied as a clear syrupy liquid.

It is commonly used in meat and poultry products to extend shelf life and improve food safety, because it inhibits most spoilage and disease-causing bacteria.

name: Calcium lactate
text:
Calcium lactate is the calcium salt of lactic acid. It has been produced industrially since the 19th century by fermenting carbohydrates in the presence of calcium carbonate or hydroxide, and contains 13% calcium.

In food it is used as a firming agent, for example to keep fresh-cut fruit firm, as a source of calcium, as a leavening aid in some baking powders, and to coagulate milk for chhena and paneer. It is also used in medicine to treat calcium deficiency.

name: Ammonium lactate
text:
Ammonium lactate is the ammonium salt of lactic acid, formed from lactic acid and ammonium hydroxide. As a food additive it is classed as an acidity regulator and flour treatment agent. It has mild antibacterial properties.

Its best-known use is outside food, as the active ingredient of moisturising lotions for dry, scaly skin.

In 1973 the FAO/WHO expert committee JECFA saw no need to limit its acceptable daily intake.

name: Magnesium lactate
text:
Magnesium lactate is the magnesium salt of lactic acid.

As a food additive it is used in foods and beverages as an acidity regulator. It is also used as a mineral supplement to prevent and treat low blood magnesium.

name: Citric acid
text:
Citric acid is a weak organic acid that occurs naturally in citrus fruits, especially lemons and limes. Almost all of it is produced industrially by fermentation: the mould Aspergillus niger is grown on a sucrose or glucose medium.

It is one of the stronger edible acids and is used mainly to give a sour taste, regulate acidity and preserve food and drinks, especially soft drinks and sweets. It is also added to ice cream to keep fats from separating and to caramel to prevent sugar crystallisation.

name: Sodium citrates
text:
Sodium citrates are the sodium salts of citric acid: monosodium, disodium and trisodium citrate. They are made by neutralising citric acid with a sodium base.

They are used as acidity regulators and buffers, as emulsifying salts that let processed cheese melt without the fat separating, and to give a tart flavour. Typical products include soft drinks, jams, sweets, ice cream, yoghurt, milk powder and processed cheese.

Trisodium citrate is also used in medicine, for example to stop stored blood from clotting.

name: Potassium citrates
text:
Potassium citrates are the potassium salts of citric acid: monopotassium and tripotassium citrate. Tripotassium citrate is made by neutralising citric acid with potassium bicarbonate, carbonate or hydroxide, and has a salty taste.

As food additives they regulate acidity, and potassium citrate is used as a buffering agent in many soft drinks. In medicine it is used to manage some types of kidney stones.

name: Calcium citrates
text:
Calcium citrates are the calcium salts of citric acid: monocalcium, dicalcium and tricalcium citrate. Calcium citrate is formed as an intermediate when citric acid is recovered from fermentation broth with lime.

As a food additive it is used mostly as a preservative and sometimes for flavour. It is also widely sold as a calcium supplement; anhydrous calcium citrate is about 24% calcium.

name: Tartaric acid
text:
Tartaric acid is an organic acid that occurs naturally in many fruits, most notably grapes, and also tamarinds and bananas. Almost all commercial tartaric acid is the natural L(+) form, obtained as a by-product of winemaking from the lees.

It is added to foods to give a distinctive sour taste and as an antioxidant.

In its 2020 re-evaluation EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake of 240 mg per kg of body weight for tartaric acid and its tartrates (E334 to E337 and E354), which estimated intakes did not exceed.

name: Sodium tartrates
text:
Sodium tartrates are the sodium salts of tartaric acid: monosodium tartrate (sodium bitartrate) and disodium tartrate. Disodium tartrate is made by reacting tartaric acid with sodium bicarbonate.

Monosodium tartrate is used as an acidity regulator. Disodium tartrate is used as an emulsifier and binding agent, for example in jellies, margarine and sausage casings.

EFSA's 2020 re-evaluation set a group acceptable daily intake of 240 mg per kg of body weight for tartaric acid and its tartrates.

name: Potassium tartrates
text:
Potassium tartrates are the potassium salts of tartaric acid: monopotassium tartrate and dipotassium tartrate. Monopotassium tartrate, known as cream of tartar, forms naturally as a crystalline deposit during winemaking and is then purified.

Cream of tartar is used as a stabiliser and acidity regulator. It is a component of baking powders, stabilises whipped egg whites for meringues and soufflés, and stops sugar syrups from crystallising.

EFSA's 2020 re-evaluation set a group acceptable daily intake of 240 mg per kg of body weight for tartaric acid and its tartrates.

name: Sodium potassium tartrate
text:
Sodium potassium tartrate, also known as Rochelle salt, is a double salt of tartaric acid. It was first prepared around 1675 by Élie Seignette, an apothecary in La Rochelle, France.

It is used in the food industry as an acidity regulator. Outside food it has been used as a laxative, in silvering mirrors and in laboratory reagents such as Fehling's solution.

EFSA's 2020 re-evaluation set a group acceptable daily intake of 240 mg per kg of body weight for tartaric acid and its tartrates.

name: Phosphoric acid
text:
Phosphoric acid is an inorganic acid produced industrially from phosphate minerals.

In food it acidifies drinks and other products such as colas and jams, giving a tangy, sour taste. It also acts as a sequestrant and as a synergist for antioxidants.

Phosphoric acid in soft drinks can contribute to dental erosion. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group maximum tolerable daily intake for phosphorus from all sources, including phosphate additives, of 70 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Sodium phosphates
text:
Sodium phosphates are sodium salts of phosphoric acid: monosodium, disodium and trisodium phosphate.

They regulate acidity and act as buffers, emulsifying salts, sequestrants and raising agents. In processed cheese they bind calcium so that the milk protein stays dispersed and the cheese does not separate when heated. They are also used in baked goods, in meat and fish products, and to retain water in frozen foods.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group maximum tolerable daily intake for phosphorus from all sources, including phosphate additives.

name: Potassium phosphates
text:
Potassium phosphates are potassium salts of phosphoric acid: monopotassium, dipotassium and tripotassium phosphate.

In food they act as buffers and sequestrants; tripotassium phosphate is also an emulsion stabiliser, and the mono- and dipotassium salts are used as yeast food.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group maximum tolerable daily intake for phosphorus from all sources, including phosphate additives.

name: Calcium phosphates
text:
Calcium phosphates are calcium salts of phosphoric acid: monocalcium, dicalcium and tricalcium phosphate. Calcium phosphates also occur naturally as minerals and in bone and tooth enamel.

In food they are used as anti-caking agents, firming agents, buffers and dough conditioners, and as yeast food.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group maximum tolerable daily intake for phosphorus from all sources, including phosphate additives.

name: Ammonium phosphates
text:
Ammonium phosphates are ammonium salts of phosphoric acid: monoammonium and diammonium phosphate. Both are widely used as agricultural fertilisers.

In food they act as acidity regulators, buffers, raising agents and dough conditioners, and as yeast food. Diammonium phosphate is also used as a yeast nutrient in winemaking.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group maximum tolerable daily intake for phosphorus from all sources, including phosphate additives.

name: Magnesium phosphates
text:
Magnesium phosphates are magnesium salts of phosphoric acid; under this number they comprise monomagnesium and dimagnesium phosphate.

In food they are used as anti-caking agents and acidity regulators, and as a source of magnesium.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group maximum tolerable daily intake for phosphorus from all sources, including phosphate additives.

name: Lecithin citrate
text: Lecithin citrate is a food additive related to lecithin and citric acid. It is classed as a preservative.

name: Magnesium citrate
text:
Magnesium citrate is a magnesium salt of citric acid. The form listed as a food additive in the EU is trimagnesium dicitrate, E345(i), added to the list in 2024. It is used as a stabiliser and anti-caking agent in solid food supplements, where it binds small amounts of residual water during processing and inside the packaging. Internationally, magnesium citrate is classed as an acidity regulator.

Outside food additive use it is a magnesium supplement and is used medicinally as a saline laxative, including to empty the bowel before a colonoscopy.

name: Ammonium malate
text:
Ammonium malate is the ammonium salt of malic acid, the acid that contributes to the sour taste of many fruits.

As a food additive, diammonium malate has been used as a flavouring agent and as an acidity regulator.

name: Sodium malates
text:
Sodium malates are sodium salts of malic acid, the acid that contributes to the sour taste of many fruits: sodium malate and sodium hydrogen malate.

They are used as acidity regulators, buffers and flavourings, for example in soft drinks and confectionery. Sodium hydrogen malate also acts as a humectant.

name: Potassium malate
text:
Potassium malate is the potassium salt of malic acid, the main acid in many fruits.

It is used as an acidity regulator and buffer, for example in canned vegetables, soups, sauces, fruit products and soft drinks. It also acts as an antioxidant and a flavouring agent.

name: Calcium malates
text:
Calcium malates are calcium salts of malic acid, the main acid in many fruits: calcium malate and calcium hydrogen malate. Calcium malate occurs naturally in maple sap.

They are used as acidity regulators, buffers and seasoning agents.

name: Metatartaric acid
text:
Metatartaric acid is a polymeric lactone of variable composition, obtained by heating tartaric acid, an acid found in grapes.

It is classed as an acidity regulator, emulsifier, stabiliser and thickener. It is added to wine to keep potassium hydrogen tartrate and calcium tartrate from crystallising out.

name: Calcium tartrate
text:
Calcium tartrate is the calcium salt of L-tartaric acid, an acid found mainly in grapes. It is a by-product of the wine industry, prepared from fermentation dregs, and can form whitish crystals in wine as it precipitates at lower temperatures.

As a food additive it is used as an acidity regulator and preservative.

name: Adipic acid
text:
Adipic acid is an organic dicarboxylic acid. It is made industrially, mainly for the production of nylon; in nature it is rare but occurs in beets.

In food it is used in small amounts as an acidity regulator, flavouring and gelling aid, and as an acidulant in baking powders, where it avoids the moisture-absorbing behaviour of tartaric acid.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 5 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Sodium adipate
text:
Sodium adipate is the sodium salt of adipic acid. It is prepared by reacting adipic acid with sodium hydroxide.

It is used as an acidity regulator and buffering agent.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 5 mg per kg of body weight for adipic acid and its sodium, potassium and ammonium salts.

name: Potassium adipate
text:
Potassium adipate is the potassium salt of adipic acid. It is used as an acidity regulator.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 5 mg per kg of body weight for adipic acid and its sodium, potassium and ammonium salts.

name: Ammonium adipate
text:
Ammonium adipate is the ammonium salt of adipic acid. It is used as an acidity regulator.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a group acceptable daily intake of 0 to 5 mg per kg of body weight for adipic acid and its sodium, potassium and ammonium salts.

name: Succinic acid
text:
Succinic acid is a dicarboxylic acid. In living organisms it occurs as succinate, an intermediate of energy metabolism. Its name comes from the Latin for amber, from which it was once obtained by distillation; today it is made chemically, for example by hydrogenation of maleic or fumaric acid.

It is used mainly as an acidity regulator, and as a flavouring that adds a somewhat sour and astringent note. In the US it is used as a flavour enhancer and pH control agent in condiments, relishes and meat products.

name: Monosodium fumarate
text:
Monosodium fumarate is a sodium salt of fumaric acid, an organic acid that occurs widely in nature, for example in fumitory, some mushrooms and lichens.

In food it acts as an acidulant, a buffering agent and a flavour enhancer.

name: Potassium fumarate
text:
Potassium fumarate is the potassium salt of fumaric acid, an organic acid that occurs widely in nature, for example in fumitory, some mushrooms and lichens.

It is used as an acidity regulator.

name: Calcium fumarate
text:
Calcium fumarate is the calcium salt of fumaric acid, an organic acid that occurs widely in nature, for example in fumitory, some mushrooms and lichens.

It is used as an acidity regulator, and has also been used to enrich foods with calcium.

name: Ammonium fumarate
text:
Ammonium fumarate is the ammonium salt of fumaric acid, an organic acid that occurs widely in nature, for example in fumitory, some mushrooms and lichens.

As a food additive it is classed as an acidity regulator.

name: 1,4-Heptonolactone
text:
1,4-Heptonolactone is a lactone, that is, a cyclic ester, of heptonic acid.

As a food additive it is classed as an acidity regulator and a sequestrant.

name: Nicotinic acid
text:
Nicotinic acid, also called niacin, is a form of vitamin B3, an essential nutrient. It is produced industrially, for example by hydrolysis of nicotinonitrile, and is used in animal feed and to fortify food.

As a food additive it is classed as a colour retention agent. High doses taken as medication can cause flushing of the skin.

name: Triammonium citrate
text:
Triammonium citrate is the triammonium salt of citric acid.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator and buffering agent. As a pure chemical it irritates the eyes, skin and airways.

name: Ammonium ferric citrate
text:
Ammonium ferric citrate is a complex salt of iron, ammonia and citric acid of undetermined structure. It occurs in a brown and a green form.

In food it is used as an anti-caking agent for salt, as an acidity regulator, for example in the Scottish soft drink Irn-Bru, and as a source of iron.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set a provisional maximum tolerable daily intake for iron from all sources of 0.8 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Calcium glycerophosphate
text:
Calcium glycerophosphate is the calcium salt of glycerophosphoric acid, a white, almost tasteless powder. It is used as a mineral supplement and is added to some toothpastes.

As a food additive it is classed as a gelling agent, stabiliser and thickener. In the US it is used as a nutrient supplement in gelatins, puddings and fillings.

name: Isopropyl citrates
text:
Isopropyl citrates are a mixture of the mono-, di- and triisopropyl esters of citric acid, made by esterifying citric acid with isopropanol.

They act as antioxidants, sequestrants and preservatives. In the US they are used in margarine, fats and oils, and non-alcoholic beverages.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 14 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Calcium disodium EDTA
text:
Calcium disodium EDTA is a salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), a synthetic chelating agent. It binds metal ions that would otherwise catalyse oxidation and discolouration.

It acts as a sequestrant, preservative, antioxidant and colour retention agent. In the US it is used, for example, in canned beans, mushrooms and seafood, pickled vegetables, mayonnaise, dressings and sauces.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 2.5 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Disodium EDTA
text:
Disodium EDTA is the disodium salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), a synthetic chelating agent. It binds metal ions that would otherwise catalyse oxidation and discolouration.

It acts as a sequestrant, preservative, antioxidant and colour stabiliser.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 2.5 mg per kg of body weight, expressed as calcium disodium EDTA, and advises that no excess disodium EDTA should remain in foods.

name: Oxystearin
text:
Oxystearin is a mixture of glycerides of partially oxidised stearic and other fatty acids, made by heating hydrogenated cottonseed or soybean oil in air with a catalyst.

It is added to vegetable oils to stop crystals forming, and also acts as a sequestrant and defoaming agent.

In 2001 the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives withdrew its acceptable daily intake and specifications for oxystearin because the additive was no longer in commercial use.

name: Thiodipropionic acid
text:
Thiodipropionic acid (3,3'-thiodipropionic acid) is a sulfur-containing dicarboxylic acid used as an antioxidant. In the US it is used in fats and oils, with the total content of antioxidants limited to 0.02 percent of the fat or oil.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 3 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Dilauryl thiodipropionate
text:
Dilauryl thiodipropionate is the dilauryl (didodecyl) ester of thiodipropionic acid. It is used as an antioxidant; in the US it is used in fats and oils, with the total content of antioxidants limited to 0.02 percent of the fat or oil.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives has set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 3 mg per kg of body weight, calculated as thiodipropionic acid.

name: Distearyl thiodipropionate
text:
Distearyl thiodipropionate is the distearyl ester of thiodipropionic acid. It is classed as an antioxidant. In the US it is listed among antioxidants that may migrate into food from packaging materials.

The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives did not extend its acceptable daily intake for thiodipropionic acid to this ester, because no specifications for it were available.

name: Phytic acid
text:
Phytic acid is the main storage form of phosphorus in plant seeds. It occurs in the hulls and kernels of nuts, grains and pulses, and in bran. It binds the minerals calcium, iron and zinc strongly and reduces their absorption; cooking, soaking, sprouting and fermentation, as in sourdough, break part of it down.

As a food additive it is used as a preservative. By binding iron it has some antioxidant effect, especially in meat, and it inhibits the enzyme that makes apples and bananas turn brown.

name: Extracts of rosemary
text:
Extracts of rosemary are obtained from the herb rosemary. Their antioxidant effect comes mainly from carnosic acid and its derivative carnosol, natural diterpenes found in rosemary and sage; dried leaves of these herbs contain 1.5 to 2.5 percent carnosic acid.

The extracts are used as antioxidant preservatives.

In 2016 the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives set a temporary acceptable daily intake of 0 to 0.3 mg per kg of body weight, expressed as carnosic acid plus carnosol.

name: Calcium lactobionate
text:
Calcium lactobionate is the calcium salt of lactobionic acid, a sugar acid formed by oxidation of lactose (milk sugar).

It is used as a stabiliser and firming agent; in the US it is used as a firming agent in dry pudding mixes.
